title: Closer to Home
summary: CDNs: beat the speed of light by moving content near your users — and keep it fresh once it's out there.

goals.text: See why distance sets a latency floor
Protect the origin with a shield
Control caching and purge stale files

steps.title: Half a world away
body: Pantry Post is a recipe site whose servers sit in Iowa. Wei opens a recipe in Singapore, 15,000 km away. Each round trip across that distance takes about 200 ms, and a page with photos needs several of them: connection, TLS, the HTML, then the images.
Her first photo appears after about 660 ms. And every viewer on Earth hits the same origin: 12,000 requests a second, most of them for the same photos.

steps.title: You can't out-code the speed of light
body: Light in optical fibre travels at about 200,000 km/s — two-thirds of its speed in a vacuum. 15,000 km takes 75 ms one way, 150 ms there and back, before any routing detour or queueing. Real paths add more.
No faster server can fix that. The only way to cut distance latency is to shorten the distance: put the content near the user.

callout.text: Each round trip pays the full distance. Distance × round trips sets a floor no hardware can beat.

steps.title: An edge server near Wei
body: A CDN (content delivery network) runs edge servers in hundreds of cities. Pantry Post points its image domain at the CDN, and Wei's requests now go to an edge in Singapore, ~5 ms away.
The first time anyone there asks for this photo, the edge doesn't have it — a miss. It fetches the photo from Iowa over a connection it keeps warm, stores a copy and returns it: 230 ms.
changes: ~ Images now served through the CDN

steps.title: Every viewer after the first
body: The next viewer in Singapore asking for that photo gets it straight from the edge: a hit. Load time falls to about 22 ms — 30× faster than going to Iowa.
Popular recipe photos are requested thousands of times a day, so most requests are now hits. The origin sees only misses: about 600 requests a second instead of 12,000.

callout.text: The best request is one that never reaches your servers.

changes: ~ Most requests hit at the edge

steps.title: Every edge misses on its own
body: Pantry Post's viewers are everywhere, so many edges are serving them — Frankfurt, São Paulo, and dozens more. Each edge has its own cache and misses on its own, and each miss crosses the world to Iowa.
When a new recipe goes viral, hundreds of edges ask the origin for the same photo within seconds. Origin load climbs back to about 4,000 req/s.

steps.title: One more layer: the origin shield
body: An origin shield is a single CDN cache placed near the origin — here, Chicago. Edges that miss ask the shield instead of the origin; only when the shield misses too does the request reach Iowa.
Now a new photo is fetched from the origin roughly once, not once per edge. Origin load falls to about 150 req/s and the overall hit ratio rises to 98%.

steps.title: The origin decides what's cacheable
body: The CDN doesn't guess: the origin labels each response with a Cache-Control header. It says whether the response may be cached, by whom, and for how long.
Photos that never change can be cached for a year. The HTML of a recipe page might be cached for a minute. A signed-in user's saved recipes must not be stored at the edge at all.

lines: # ETag lets an edge revalidate cheaply

steps.title: Same name, new picture
body: Pantry Post rebrands and uploads a new logo — to the same URL, /logo.png, which was cached for a week. Edges that already have the old file keep serving it until it expires.
Viewers see a mix of old and new logos for days, depending on which edge they hit.
changes: ~ Logo replaced at the same URL

steps.title: Purge — or change the name
body: Most CDNs offer a purge: an API call telling every edge to drop a URL, which takes effect within seconds. It's the emergency tool.

The everyday fix is versioned URLs: name files after their contents, like logo.3f9a.png. A new logo gets a new name, pages link to it, and both files can be cached forever — nothing stale is ever served.

steps.title: What the edge can't cache
body: Personal pages — Wei's saved recipes, her shopping list — can't be cached; they must come from the origin. But the CDN still helps: Wei's TLS handshake finishes at the nearby edge in a few milliseconds, and the edge forwards her request over a connection to the origin that's already open.
That saves the extra round trips across the ocean, even though the request itself still has to make the long trip once.

callout.text: A CDN helps uncacheable requests too, by ending TLS nearby and reusing long-haul connections.

changes: + Personal request passes through the edge

steps.title: Closer to home
body:
• Distance sets a latency floor: ~1 ms per 100 km of round trip, per round trip.
  • CDN edges cache content near users; hits skip the long haul entirely.
  • An origin shield collapses many edge misses into one origin fetch.
  • Cache-Control headers decide what is cached and for how long.
  • Versioned URLs avoid stale files; purge is the emergency brake.
